title: Diffraction

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain the meaning of the term diffraction, and understand experiments that demonstrate it, including the qualitative effect of the gap width relative to the wavelength of the wave.

blocks.heading: What diffraction is
blocks.text: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or past the edge of an obstacle. The wave stays in the same medium: its speed, frequency and wavelength are unchanged; what changes is the set of directions in which the wave energy travels. Each point of a wavefront that survives at the gap sends wave energy onward into new directions, which is why the wavefront beyond a narrow gap curves outward. (A point's displacement — its distance from its rest position — carries on oscillating at the same frequency throughout.) The spreading is not refraction: refraction is the change of direction at a boundary where the wave's speed changes.

blocks.heading: The gap relative to the wavelength
blocks.text: How much a wave spreads depends on the ratio of the gap width to the wavelength. The spreading is greatest when the gap is close to one wavelength wide. A gap several wavelengths wide lets the middle of the wavefront through almost straight, with slight curving at the two edges. A gap much narrower than a wavelength passes little energy, though what passes spreads widely. The same rule applies at an obstacle's edge: a wave spreads around it appreciably when the obstacle's size is comparable to the wavelength.

blocks.heading: A ripple tank shows diffraction
blocks.text: A ripple tank has a vibrating bar that makes straight wavefronts. A barrier with a gap is placed in their path, and the wavefronts beyond the gap are viewed against the tank's shadow grid. With the gap set about one wavelength wide, the wavefronts beyond it spread into wide, nearly semicircular arcs. The gap is then widened to several wavelengths, and the wavefronts beyond stay nearly straight apart from curving at the edges. The wavelength is read against the grid so the gap width can be set as a stated multiple of it, and the comparison of the two patterns shows the effect of the ratio.

blocks.heading: Behind the wall, and behind the hill
blocks.text: Diffraction explains why waves carry round obstacles. A minibus taxi's horn in a Windhoek street is heard from behind a concrete wall: the horn's low notes have wavelengths of a metre or so, comparable to the wall, so the sound spreads around its edge and reaches the pavement beyond. The same physics separates radio from light: a radio beacon of wavelength 1.2 km serves fishing boats behind a rocky headland about a kilometre across, because the radio wave spreads appreciably around an obstacle of comparable size; the harbour lantern on the same headland, with a wavelength of order 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, spreads far too little on that scale to be seen around it and travels on in straight lines.

blocks.heading: Diffraction is not refraction
blocks.text: A learner who says a wave 'bends because it enters shallower water' has described refraction. Diffraction happens in one medium with no change of speed; refraction happens at a boundary between two media of different speeds. The test: does the wave change medium? If it does not, any spreading at a gap or an edge is diffraction; if it does, the bending is refraction.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Diffraction is one of the two behaviours that follow from superposition (8.1); the two-source interference patterns of 8.3 are seen at all because each slit's waves diffract before they overlap. Topic 7 supplies the wavelength of each region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
